segments.t: Configure terminal display and behavior settings, including dimensions, scrollback, character encoding, keyword highlighting, links, paste protection, shell integration, and SSH connection management. Open via KTPH001Configuration → Global Settings → TerminalKTPH002; stored in KTPH000.
Compress the scrollback in the background while idle
Bold font, Bright colors, Bold font and bright colors
Allow drag and drop into the terminal (files copy over SFTP, text is pasted)
Let programs in the terminal copy text to the clipboard (OSC 52)
Close active terminal windows without confirmation
Also highlight in full-screen programs (vim, less, htop)
None, Errors and warnings, Network addresses, Network devices, or a set of your own
Run actions of highlight rules (notifications, snippets)
Detect web addresses, e-mail addresses and file paths in terminal text
2–26 different lowercase letters KTPH000–KTPH001; empty for the default
up to 16 regular expressions of up to 512 characters each
Off, Unless the program uses bracketed paste, Always
Unless the program uses bracketed paste
Use the command marks of shells set up for shell integration (OSC 133)
opens the window with the shell snippets
KTPH000 (width: KTPH001, 200–1,200, default 300) — see KTPH002Remote files sidebarKTPH003
Disable host key verification for all connections

Detect coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, MiniMax Code, Qwen Code, OpenCode, Cursor Agent, Aider, Amp, Goose, Crush, Kiro CLI, Continue, Grok CLI, Jules, GitHub Copilot CLI, Grok Build, Antigravity CLI, Cline) in local shell tabs
Automatically show and hide the coding-agent sidebar
Show the number of agents waiting for a decision on the app icon
Allow a local program to read and control this korTTY
Desktop notification preferences, including coding-agent messages, are on the separate KTPH000MessagingKTPH001 page.

The character encoding korTTY decodes the output of an SSH session with and encodes what you type and paste in. It applies to every SSH connection that does not choose its own KTPH002Character encodingKTPH003 on the KTPH004ConnectionKTPH005 tab of the connection editor (see KTPH006Character encodingKTPH007). Local shells use UTF-8 unless their connection sets an encoding, and Mosh always uses UTF-8 because mosh-server and mosh-client require it. Pick the encoding the programs on the server actually write, usually what KTPH000 reports there. A change applies the next time a tab connects or reconnects; open tabs keep their encoding. Characters the chosen encoding cannot represent are sent as KTPH001.

Earlier versions ignored this setting, so a value chosen back then is not applied on its own: SSH sessions stay UTF-8, and a note under the dropdown says so, until you save the settings after opening the Terminal page. Choose KTPH000UTF-8KTPH001 before saving if you do not want the old value.

Sets how text that a program prints in bold is drawn. KTPH000Bold fontKTPH001 (the default) draws it in a bold font in its own color. KTPH002Bright colorsKTPH003 draws bold text in one of the 8 basic ANSI colors in the matching bright color of the palette instead, in the normal font weight, the way xterm does: bold red becomes bright red. KTPH004Bold font and bright colorsKTPH005 does both. Only the 8 basic colors are brightened, including colors 0–7 that a program selects from the 256-color table; the default text color, the bright colors, the other 256 colors and true colors stay as they are. The bright colors come from the palette on the KTPH006ColorsKTPH007 tab, so a customized palette applies. Inverse bold text gets a bright background, while the selection, search-match and link highlight colors never change. A saved change applies to every open terminal at once, and terminal recordings with KTPH008Capture terminal colors in recordingsKTPH009 use the same colors as the screen. Settings files from before this option load as KTPH010Bold fontKTPH011; the earlier KTPH012Bold as bright colorKTPH013 switch affected recordings only and is no longer used.

KTPH000ScrollbackKTPH001 sets how many lines of output each terminal pane keeps in its scrollback buffer. The value is read when a terminal is created, so a change applies to newly opened tabs and split panes — already-open terminals keep their current line count.

KTPH000Scrollback memoryKTPH001 sets the most memory the scrollback of one pane may use, from 1 to 50 MB. Whichever limit a pane reaches first, the line count or the memory, drops its oldest lines. The memory is an estimate of what the lines take up in korTTY's Java heap. A saved change also applies to open terminals: lowering the limit drops the oldest lines of every open pane at once.

With KTPH001Compress the scrollback in the background while idleKTPH002, korTTY packs the scrollback lines that are not on screen into compressed blocks once a terminal has had no output for about one and a half seconds. It works in the background, a few milliseconds at a time, so the same memory holds several times as many lines: in our measurements, 100,000 lines of KTPH000 or log output took 7 to 9 MB instead of 59 to 67 MB. The lines on screen, a screenful around them and the newest screenful of the scrollback stay unpacked, and nothing is packed while the find bar shows results. A packed line is unpacked as soon as you scroll to it or search the scrollback. When the scrollback of a terminal reaches its memory limit, older lines are packed first and only then dropped. A saved change also applies to open terminals; switching compression off leaves packed lines packed until they are shown.
Settings files from before these two options load with 10 MB and compression on.

When enabled, text you select in a terminal is copied to the clipboard as soon as you select it. On Linux it also becomes the X11 primary selection, so a middle-click pastes it in other applications such as xterm or gedit. With the enterprise policy's KTPH000internal clipboard modeKTPH001 the selection stays inside korTTY on every platform.

With KTPH000Let programs in the terminal copy text to the clipboard (OSC 52)KTPH001 on, programs such as vim, Neovim and tmux, also on a server over SSH, can put up to 256 KiB of text at a time on your clipboard with the OSC 52 escape sequence, and the status bar names the tab each time. They can never read the clipboard, because korTTY never answers the OSC 52 query. It is off by default, because any program whose output reaches the terminal could replace what you copied; while it is off, the status bar says when a program tried. With the enterprise policy's KTPH002internal clipboard modeKTPH003 what programs copy stays inside korTTY. The setting is read on every write, so a change applies to open tabs as soon as you save. See KTPH004Programs copying to the clipboardKTPH005.

KTPH006Highlight keywords in terminal outputKTPH007 is the master switch of KTPH008keyword highlightingKTPH009. While it is off, no pane is highlighted, whatever was chosen in a menu, with KTPH010KTPH000KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH001KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH002KTPH015 (KTPH016KTPH003KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH004KTPH019+KTPH020KTPH005KTPH021 on macOS), for a connection or as the default rule set, and the highlighting menus are greyed out. It is on by default, but nothing is highlighted until a rule set is chosen.

KTPH000Default rule setKTPH001 is the set every terminal pane shows unless its connection has a rule set of its own (see KTPH002Rule set per connectionKTPH003) or you choose another one for that pane. It is KTPH004NoneKTPH005 by default, so highlighting stays off until you opt in here, for a connection in the connection editor, in KTPH006View → HighlightingKTPH007, in a pane's context menu or with the shortcut. A set chosen for a pane in one of those places stays on top of the default until the pane is closed, and KTPH008NoneKTPH009 chosen there keeps that pane plain whatever the default is. If the stored default names a rule set that no longer exists, the dropdown shows it as missing and panes show no highlighting.

KTPH003Also highlight in full-screen programsKTPH004 extends highlighting to programs that use the terminal's alternate screen, such as KTPH000, KTPH001 and KTPH002. It is off by default because these programs redraw their screen constantly and bring their own colors, so highlights can flicker there and fight the program's colors. Switching it off leaves the highlights a running program already shows until it redraws them.
All three apply to open terminals as soon as you save.

KTPH000Edit Rules…KTPH001 opens the KTPH002rule-set editorKTPH003, where you create your own rule sets and look at the built-in ones. It stays available while the master switch is off, so you can prepare sets before switching highlighting on. The editor saves its changes when you confirm it, whether or not you then save the settings dialog, and afterwards the KTPH004Default rule setKTPH005 dropdown lists your sets as they are now. If you delete the set the dropdown shows, it falls back to KTPH006NoneKTPH007.

KTPH001Run actions of highlight rules (notifications, snippets)KTPH002 lets rules whose action is KTPH003Desktop notificationKTPH004 mark their tab and notify when their pattern appears in new output in a tab you are not looking at (see KTPH005Notifications for matching outputKTPH006), and rules whose action is KTPH007Run a snippetKTPH008 run their snippet in the pane where the pattern appears, after asking you once per connection (see KTPH009Running a snippet when output matchesKTPH010). It is on by default, because a rule only gets an action when you give it one; switched off, such rules only highlight. It is greyed out while the master switch is off, and it is read on every match, so a change applies to open terminals as soon as you save. The enterprise policy key KTPH000 locks it in the position the policy chose (see KTPH011Enterprise policyKTPH012).

With KTPH002Detect web addresses, e-mail addresses and file paths in terminal textKTPH003 on, KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005 + click (macOS) or KTPH006KTPH001KTPH007 + click (Windows, Linux) opens a web address, an e-mail address or a file path that a program printed as plain text: a web address in your default browser, an e-mail address as a new mail in your mail program, and in SSH and local-shell tabs a file path as text in the Snippet Editor. A plain click still only selects text. A change applies to the open terminals at once. Links that a program marks up itself with OSC 8 open with the same click either way. See KTPH008Links in terminal outputKTPH009.

KTPH003Quick select label lettersKTPH004 and KTPH005Quick select patternsKTPH006 adjust KTPH007quick selectKTPH008 (KTPH009Edit → Quick SelectKTPH010): the letters its labels are made of, in the order they are used, and regular expressions, one per line, whose matches it labels too, such as ticket numbers or host names. The letters must be at least two different lowercase letters from KTPH000 to KTPH001, because KTPH011KTPH002KTPH012 with a label opens its match and every other key ends quick select; leave the field empty for the default. Up to 16 patterns of up to 512 characters each are accepted, and blank lines are skipped. A problem, such as a pattern that is not a valid regular expression, one that also matches empty text or holds an invisible control character, a repeated letter or an uppercase one, is explained in red under its field, with the line number for a pattern, and KTPH013SaveKTPH014 keeps the dialog open until it is corrected. A pattern that takes too long on what the screen shows is skipped for that quick select instead of holding up the window. Both apply the next time quick select starts; see KTPH015Your own patterns and label lettersKTPH016.

Decides which terminal pastes ask before they reach the pane; the dialog itself is described under KTPH006Paste protectionKTPH007. KTPH008Warn about multi-line pastesKTPH009 decides when a paste with a line break asks: KTPH010Unless the program uses bracketed pasteKTPH011 (the default) asks only when the program in the pane would receive each line break as Enter, KTPH012AlwaysKTPH013 asks for every paste with a line break, and KTPH014OffKTPH015 never asks. Whenever it is not KTPH016OffKTPH017, a paste with control characters (such as Escape or Ctrl+C) or with invisible characters that change the text direction asks too, bracketed or not. KTPH018Warn about pastes larger thanKTPH019 asks for every paste above that size in KiB, whatever the dropdown says; 0 turns the size check off. Both apply to the next paste. They are stored as KTPH000 (KTPH001, KTPH002 or KTPH003; an unknown value counts as KTPH004) and KTPH005. A connection can choose its own warning and pause in the KTPH020Terminal behaviorKTPH021 section of the connection editor, which then wins for its panes; the size check always comes from here (see KTPH022Paste protection per connectionKTPH023).

KTPH002Pause after each pasted lineKTPH003 is for devices such as switches, routers and console servers that lose input arriving too fast: a paste with several lines is sent one line at a time, with this many milliseconds after each line. While it runs, the pane takes no keyboard input and KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005 stops the paste (see KTPH006Pasting into slow devicesKTPH007). 0 sends every paste at once. It is stored as KTPH000.

Whether a program uses bracketed paste is what the server reports, and any output can switch it on, also in a shell such as KTPH000 that does not handle it. Pasted line breaks then run without a warning, so choose KTPH001AlwaysKTPH002 if you work on production servers.

With KTPH013Use the command marks of shells set up for shell integration (OSC 133)KTPH014 on, korTTY reads the invisible marks that a shell with korTTY's snippet in its startup file prints around every prompt and command, and KTPH015KTPH001KTPH016+KTPH017KTPH002KTPH018+KTPH019KTPH003KTPH020 / KTPH021KTPH004KTPH022+KTPH023KTPH005KTPH024+KTPH025KTPH006KTPH026 (KTPH027KTPH007KTPH028+KTPH029KTPH008KTPH030+KTPH031KTPH009KTPH032 / KTPH033KTPH010KTPH034+KTPH035KTPH011KTPH036+KTPH037KTPH012KTPH038 on Windows and Linux), KTPH039Edit → Previous Prompt / Next PromptKTPH040 and the terminal's right-click menu jump between the prompts. The snippets for bash, zsh and fish are on the KTPH041Shell integrationKTPH042 page, and KTPH043Set Up Shell Integration…KTPH044 opens a window with them and a KTPH045CopyKTPH046 button, also while the setting is off. Without a snippet in the shell's startup file nothing changes. The marks also tell korTTY that an SSH session is at its prompt, for the AI Agent's KTPH000 commands and the question before closing a busy tab; this setting replaces KTPH047Use OSC 133 prompt markers when the shell already provides themKTPH048, which KTPH049AI → AI Manager → GeneralKTPH050 used to show and which changed nothing. Switched off, the prompt keys reach the program in the terminal, the right-click menu has no shell-integration entries, and korTTY tells that a session is at its prompt from the prompt's text alone. The setting is read on every mark and key press, so a change applies to open tabs as soon as you save.

For local shell tabs, a connection can also add the snippet by itself: KTPH000Add shell integration automaticallyKTPH001 in the connection editor starts bash, zsh or fish with korTTY's shell integration and leaves your startup files unchanged. It needs this setting on; see KTPH002Adding it to local shells automaticallyKTPH003.

When enabled, korTTY sends periodic keep-alive packets to prevent SSH sessions from timing out during idle periods. The interval setting controls how often (in seconds) these packets are sent. The spinner range is 5–600 seconds; the interval is disabled if SSH Keep-Alive is toggled off.
Disable host key verification for all connections

This is the global, lowest-precedence host-key setting: it relaxes verification to accept-new for every connection that does not set its own or its group's override. Accept-new still hard-blocks a changed key on a host already pinned, and a jump server's own key is always verified strictly — but disabling first-use verification removes protection against a man-in-the-middle on the very first connection. Off by default. Per-connection and per-group overrides are set in the Connection Manager; see KTPH000Security → Relaxing host-key verificationKTPH001.
Drag and drop into the terminal

When enabled, you can drop files or folders from your file manager (Finder on macOS, Explorer on Windows) directly into the terminal window. The files will be copied to the remote SSH server via SFTP.

Text dropped onto a terminal pane, from a browser, an editor or another korTTY window, is pasted into the pane under the pointer, through KTPH000paste protectionKTPH001 like any other paste; see KTPH002Dropping textKTPH003. A drag that carries files and their path as text copies the files. With the enterprise policy's KTPH004internal clipboard modeKTPH005, text dragged from another application is refused. When this setting is off, the terminal takes neither files nor text.
When enabled, a sidebar appears on the left side of the terminal displaying the date and time each command was entered, useful for audit trails and session logging.

Each mark stays on its command line when the scrollback is full and the oldest lines are dropped, and a mark whose line has left the scrollback disappears with it. KTPH005Clear BufferKTPH006 in the terminal's right-click menu, and a KTPH000 that also empties the scrollback, remove all marks; the next command gets a fresh one. Opening and quitting a full-screen program such as KTPH001 or KTPH002 does not move the marks. The day and month above each mark and the full date in the hover popup follow the korTTY UI language (for example KTPH003 in German, KTPH004 in English), as does the elapsed time in the popup.

In a shell set up for KTPH000shell integrationKTPH001, the sidebar also shows how each command ended: ✓ for exit status 0, ✗ for any other and … while it runs, with the command's real runtime next to the date and the exit status in the hover popup. The time such a command finished comes from the shell instead of from the first half second without output. The exit statuses are not saved with a project; the timestamps are.
When enabled, failed SSH connections are automatically retried. Disabling this prevents automatic reconnection attempts for failed connections.

Retries only cover failures that a further attempt could resolve. A changed host key, a refused login, an SSH key file that is missing or cannot be read, a jump server whose stored password cannot be used or whose setup is incomplete, a Mosh connection configured with a jump server, or a missing Mosh runtime is refused immediately regardless of this setting.

When enabled and an KTPH000establishedKTPH001 SSH connection is lost (network drop, server gone), the tab reconnects on its own with increasing delays — 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, then every 60 seconds — and the red status bar counts down to the next attempt. A double-click on the bar still reconnects immediately, and a successful reconnect or closing the tab stops the automatic attempts. Failed logins and other permanent failures (authentication, host key, configuration) are never retried automatically, and a connection that never got established is not retried by this setting either — that is what KTPH002Enable connection retriesKTPH003 covers. See KTPH004Terminal sessions → Connection lossKTPH005.
Allow a local program to read and control this korTTY

This is the Control API, and it is the only setting in this tab that is off by default. While it is on, any program running under your user account on this computer can list your windows, read every open pane — local shells and SSH sessions alike — and type into them, including pressing KTPH002KTPH001KTPH003. Nothing is reachable over the network and no other user of the computer can connect, but that is the extent of the boundary: within your own account it is the same power as sitting at your keyboard. A status line under the checkbox reports what the listener is actually doing, because the checkbox and the listener can legitimately disagree — enterprise policy can deny the feature, and a start can fail because another korTTY already owns the socket. Every action is logged with byte counts only, never terminal text, and the first time a program types into a pane you get one desktop notification. See KTPH004Control APIKTPH005 for the security model and KTPH006Control CLIKTPH007 for the KTPH000 client that speaks it.

KTPH002MCP serverKTPH003 and KTPH004Allow write toolsKTPH005 below it let an AI assistant reach korTTY through KTPH000: the first offers read-only tools with secrets masked and output capped, the second adds tools that type into a pane, each of which korTTY asks you about first. Both are off by default, greyed out while the Control API is off and locked when the enterprise policy denies KTPH001. See KTPH006MCP clientsKTPH007.

When enabled, korTTY watches every local shell pane for a running Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, MiniMax Code, Qwen Code, OpenCode, Cursor Agent, Aider, Amp, Goose, Crush, Kiro CLI, Continue, Grok CLI, Jules, GitHub Copilot CLI, Grok Build, Antigravity CLI or Cline and tracks whether it is working, blocked on a question, done or idle. The screen is analysed locally and nothing leaves the computer; the change applies immediately to open tabs. The other two toggles in this section control automatic sidebar visibility and the count of waiting agents on the app icon (or in the window title where no icon badge exists). Coding-agent desktop notifications are controlled separately under KTPH000MessagingKTPH001; all changes apply to open sessions when you save. See KTPH002Coding agentsKTPH003.
